questions.q: What kind of course is Engineering 503 B, Physics One?
options: A laboratory substitute for a full semester of 8.01
A Brief course: an overview of about five minutes plus six lectures of about ten minutes, about an hour in all, and the first physics Foundations course in Anderson Engineering
The same course as Calculus One
A course in electricity and magnetism
questions.explain: Paragraph 0.1 states the course code, the Brief format, and its place in Anderson Engineering. A is wrong: A Brief course is not a substitute for a semester. C is wrong: Calculus One is Engineering 501 B, the mathematical companion. D is wrong: That would be Physics Two, after 8.02.

questions.q: The map of this course follows the weekly spine of which MIT subject?
options: 18.01SC, Single Variable Calculus
8.01SC, Classical Mechanics
8.02, Electricity and Magnetism, only
A course in thermodynamics only
questions.explain: Paragraph 0.5: The overview says the map follows the weekly spine of MIT's 8.01SC. A is wrong: That is the backbone of Calculus One. C is wrong: 8.02 is named as a sequel, not as this course's spine. D is wrong: Thermodynamics is not the spine of this map.

questions.q: What are the stated prerequisites, and what is the natural mathematical companion?
options: A prior licence in professional engineering
Engineering 504 B, Physics Two, must be taken first
No mathematics of any kind
High school algebra and trigonometry; Engineering 501 B, Calculus One, is the natural mathematical companion
questions.explain: Paragraph 0.7 states those prerequisites and names 501 B as the companion. A is wrong: These are knowledge courses, not a path to a licence. B is wrong: 504 B follows this course, it does not precede it. C is wrong: Algebra and trigonometry are required, and calculus is the companion.

questions.q: What is the backbone of this course?
options: MIT OpenCourseWare 8.01SC, Classical Mechanics, as taught in Fall 2016 by Professor Deepto Chakrabarty, Dr Peter Dourmashkin, Dr Michelle Tomasik, Professor Anna Frebel and Professor Vladan Vuletic
MIT 18.01SC, as taught by David Jerison in 2010
A copied official MIT examination, used verbatim
An uncredited set of problem-set solutions
questions.explain: Paragraph 0.9: The overview names that course, that term, and those instructors, under a Creative Commons licence, with original wording here. B is wrong: That is the backbone of Calculus One. C is wrong: The wording of this Brief course is original to the Academy. D is wrong: The source is named and credited.

questions.q: What is kinematics, as this lecture uses the word?
options: The description of motion, without yet asking what causes the motion to change
The study of forces that cause motion
The study of energy and work only
The study of rotating rigid bodies only
questions.explain: Paragraph 1.1: The opening paragraph defines kinematics in exactly those terms. B is wrong: That is dynamics, which begins in lecture two. C is wrong: Work and energy are lecture five. D is wrong: Rotation is lecture six; kinematics begins with particles and points.

questions.q: What is average velocity on a time interval?
options: Speed added to acceleration
Displacement divided by the time elapsed
The slope of an acceleration-time graph
The second derivative of position
questions.explain: Paragraph 1.3: The lecture defines average velocity as that quotient, and illustrates it with a car covering 100 metres. A is wrong: Velocity is not a sum of speed and acceleration. C is wrong: The slope of a v–t graph is acceleration; average velocity is Δx/Δt. D is wrong: That is acceleration, once the derivatives exist.

questions.q: When acceleration is constant, which of these is a kinematic relation given in the lecture?
options: v = v₀ t, and x = ½ a only
x = v t² for every motion
a = x t, always
v = v₀ + at, and x = x₀ + v₀ t + ½ at²
questions.explain: Paragraph 1.5: The lecture says these constant-acceleration equations are worth knowing by heart. A is wrong: Those formulas are incomplete or wrong. B is wrong: That is not a general law, even for constant a. C is wrong: Acceleration is the derivative of velocity, not the product x t.

questions.q: What is a unit vector, and how is a velocity written in components?
options: A unit vector has length equal to the speed
Components cannot be used in two dimensions
A unit vector names a direction and has length 1; v is written as v_x in the x direction plus v_y in the y direction
A unit vector is the same as a force
questions.explain: Paragraph 1.8: The lecture defines unit vectors and the component form of v in those terms. A is wrong: Its length is 1, not the speed. B is wrong: The lecture's point is that they can, and must. D is wrong: It is a direction, not a force.

questions.q: In projectile motion near the Earth, neglecting air resistance, what is the acceleration?
options: Zero horizontally, and minus g vertically, if upward is chosen as positive
g horizontally and zero vertically
A centripetal acceleration toward the thrower
Zero in both directions after the ball leaves the hand
questions.explain: Paragraph 1.9: The lecture states that standard two-dimensional application in those terms. B is wrong: Those components are reversed. C is wrong: A projectile is not in uniform circular motion about the thrower. D is wrong: Vertical acceleration remains g throughout the flight, in this model.

questions.q: How are relative velocities combined in the lecture's boat example?
options: By multiplying the two speeds
By vector addition: the velocity of the boat relative to the ground is the velocity relative to the water plus the velocity of the water relative to the ground
By subtracting the masses of boat and river
By dividing displacement by g
questions.explain: Paragraph 1.11: The lecture introduces relative velocity as v_AC = v_AB + v_BC, with a boat in a current as the example. A is wrong: Velocities add as vectors, they are not multiplied. C is wrong: Mass does not enter kinematics. D is wrong: That is not relative velocity.

questions.q: On a graph of x versus t, what is the slope, and what is the area under a graph of v versus t?
options: The slope is the acceleration, and the area is the mass
Both are the jerk, the derivative of acceleration
The slope is position, and the area is time
The slope is the velocity; the area under v versus t is the displacement Δx
questions.explain: Paragraph 1.12: The lecture says graphs are part of the language, with those two readings. A is wrong: Acceleration is the slope of v versus t, not of x versus t. B is wrong: The lecture does not assign that meaning to those graphs. C is wrong: Those identifications are reversed or wrong.

questions.q: What does Newton's first law say?
options: The net force equals mass times acceleration
Forces come in pairs
A body remains at rest, or in motion at constant velocity in a straight line, unless a net force acts on it
Every body eventually stops, even if no force acts
questions.explain: Paragraph 2.2: The lecture states the first law in those terms, and ties it to inertial frames. A is wrong: That is the second law. B is wrong: That is the third law. D is wrong: The first law denies that everyday intuition.

questions.q: What is Newton's second law, in the form the lecture calls its quantitative core?
options: Force is equal to mass times velocity
Every force has an equal and opposite partner on the same body
Acceleration is independent of force
The net force on a body equals the rate of change of its momentum, which is ma when the mass is constant
questions.explain: Paragraph 2.3: The lecture gives F_net = dp/dt, and ma for constant mass. A is wrong: That would be a confusion with momentum. B is wrong: Third-law partners act on different bodies. C is wrong: The second law ties them together.

questions.q: What does Newton's third law say about two bodies A and B?
options: If A exerts a force on B, then B exerts an equal and opposite force on A
The two forces in a pair both act on body A
The net force on a system is always twice the larger force
A force can exist on A with no partner
questions.explain: Paragraph 2.4: The lecture states the third law as that pairing. B is wrong: The partners act on different bodies; that is a later caution of the lecture. C is wrong: Internal third-law pairs cancel in the net force on the system. D is wrong: The third law says forces come in pairs.

questions.q: What is the working method called a force diagram in this lecture?
options: Draw every force in the universe on one figure
Draw only the motion arrows, never the forces
Replace every force by a potential energy at the outset
Isolate one body or system, draw every force that acts on it, and do not draw forces that the body exerts on something else
questions.explain: Paragraph 2.5: The lecture gives that method, and then writes ΣF_x = ma_x and ΣF_y = ma_y. A is wrong: The method isolates one chosen system. B is wrong: The diagram is a diagram of forces. C is wrong: Potential energy belongs to lecture five.

questions.q: What is the normal force, as the lecture defines it?
options: The component of the contact force perpendicular to the surface
The body's weight, in every situation
The tension in a string
A force that acts only at a distance, like gravity
questions.explain: Paragraph 2.7: The lecture distinguishes the normal force from the parallel (frictional) component of contact. B is wrong: Weight is the gravitational force; the normal force may differ from it, as in an accelerating lift. C is wrong: Tension is treated in the next paragraph. D is wrong: The normal force is a contact force.

questions.q: For an ideal massless string, what is true of the tension?
options: The tension is always equal to the weight of the heavier mass, at every instant
The tension acts on only one end
The tension is a property of gravity alone
The tension is the same along the string
questions.explain: Paragraph 2.8: The lecture states that property of an ideal massless string. A is wrong: In an Atwood machine the tension is not equal to either weight while the masses accelerate. B is wrong: Each end exerts a tension on the body attached there. C is wrong: Tension is a contact force in the string.

questions.q: How does the lecture distinguish static friction from kinetic friction?
options: Both are always equal to μ N, whether or not the surfaces slip
Static friction acts to prevent slipping and can vary up to a maximum μ_s N; kinetic friction is μ_k N, directed against the slipping
Static friction exists only in liquids
Kinetic friction speeds a sliding body up
questions.explain: Paragraph 2.9: The lecture states those two laws of friction. A is wrong: Static friction is only at most μ_s N, and is not a fixed value. C is wrong: The lecture treats contact between solid surfaces. D is wrong: It is directed against the slipping, so it opposes the sliding.

questions.q: In Atwood's machine, with masses 3 kg and 5 kg over an ideal pulley, what is the form of the acceleration?
options: a = (m₁ − m₂) g / (m₁ + m₂)
a = g, as if both masses were falling under gravity alone, with no string
a = 0, because the pulley never turns
a = (m₁ + m₂) g / (m₁ − m₂)
questions.explain: Paragraph 2.11: The lecture gives that standard arrangement and that result. B is wrong: The string and the second mass reduce the acceleration below g. C is wrong: The unequal masses accelerate. D is wrong: The numerator and denominator are reversed.

questions.q: A person stands in a lift that starts upward from rest. What happens to the apparent weight, the reading of a scale?
options: The scale always reads mg, because weight is constant
The normal force N satisfies N − mg = ma_lift, so the scale reading is larger than mg while the lift accelerates upward
The scale reads zero whenever the lift is above the ground floor
The person's mass changes during the start
questions.explain: Paragraph 2.15: The lecture's question is that elevator (lift) example, using N − mg = ma. A is wrong: Weight mg is constant; the scale reads N, which can differ from mg. C is wrong: That would be true if the lift were falling with acceleration g, not in an upward acceleration. D is wrong: Mass does not change; the normal force does.

questions.q: For motion at speed v on a circle of radius r, what acceleration is always present?
options: An acceleration toward the centre of magnitude v²/r
An outward acceleration of magnitude mv
A tangential acceleration of v²/r, even when speed is constant
Zero acceleration, because speed is constant
questions.explain: Paragraph 3.2: The lecture states that inward, or centripetal, acceleration as a kinematic fact. B is wrong: There is no outward acceleration of that form; the acceleration of circular motion is inward. C is wrong: v²/r is radial; a tangential component appears only when the speed is changing. D is wrong: Constant speed on a curve still means a changing velocity, hence an acceleration.

questions.q: If the speed on a curved path is also changing, what second component of acceleration appears?
options: A component of magnitude g, always directed outward
A tangential component a_t = dv/dt, with the total acceleration the combination of the radial and tangential parts
A component that cancels v²/r exactly
No second component; acceleration has only one possible direction
questions.explain: Paragraph 3.3: The lecture adds that tangential component when speed is not constant. A is wrong: The tangential component is along the path, and is not automatically g. C is wrong: The radial part remains v²/r even when a tangential part is present. D is wrong: The lecture's point is that there are then two components.

questions.q: On a frictionless banked curve of angle θ, what provides the inward force?
options: A separate new force called the centripetal force, added by hand
Friction alone, because the surface is frictionless
The horizontal component of the normal force, N sin θ, equals m v²/R when the banking is matched to the speed
The car's weight, directed horizontally
questions.explain: Paragraph 3.5: The lecture describes banking in those terms. A is wrong: The lecture later warns that centripetal acceleration is not a third force to add. B is wrong: The surface is described as frictionless; banking, not friction, supplies the inward component. D is wrong: Weight is vertical.

questions.q: What supplies the inward force for a satellite in a circular orbit, in this lecture?
options: A normal force from the vacuum
Air resistance
Gravity, with GMm/r² = m v²/r
The satellite's engines, which must fire continuously
questions.explain: Paragraph 3.6: The lecture says orbital motion is the same law, with gravity as the inward force. A is wrong: There is no surface to supply a normal force in orbit. B is wrong: Drag is treated later, and is not what holds a satellite in a circular orbit. D is wrong: A circular orbit is modelled here as gravity providing the required inward acceleration.

questions.q: How does the lecture describe resistive forces at low speed and at higher speed?
options: Drag is always a constant, independent of speed
Drag is a gravitational force, equal to mg
Drag exists only in circular motion
At low speeds in a viscous fluid, drag is often approximately linear in v; at higher speeds it is often quadratic, of the form c v²
questions.explain: Paragraph 3.9: The lecture gives those two common models. A is wrong: The point is that drag depends on velocity. B is wrong: Drag is a resistive force, not weight. C is wrong: Drag is treated as a general velocity-dependent force.

questions.q: A body falling under gravity with quadratic air drag does not keep accelerating at g. What happens instead?
options: Drag eventually reverses gravity, and the body rises
The mass decreases until the acceleration is zero
As speed grows, drag grows, and the body approaches a terminal speed at which mg = c v_t²
The acceleration remains g, but the distance formula changes
questions.explain: Paragraph 3.10: The lecture gives that account and that expression for v_t. A is wrong: Terminal speed is a downward balance, not a reversal. B is wrong: Mass is not the mechanism in this paragraph. D is wrong: The point of the paragraph is that acceleration does not remain g.

questions.q: On a rainy day, the coefficient of friction on a level curve is reduced. What is the danger the lecture's question is pointing to?
options: The car's mass suddenly changes
Gravity is weaker in the rain
The radius of the curve increases when it rains
The maximum available inward friction μ N may fall below the m v²/R required for the curve, so the car can leave the path
questions.explain: Paragraph 3.15: The lecture's question is about a level road whose friction is reduced by rain. A is wrong: Mass is not what the rain changes. B is wrong: Gravity is unchanged. C is wrong: The radius is a property of the road, not of the weather.

questions.q: How is Newton's second law written at the opening of this lecture, and why is that form more general?
options: F_net equals m v, which is already general
F_net equals the rate of change of momentum, which remains valid when mass is not constant
F_net equals zero in every collision
F_net equals the integral of position
questions.explain: Paragraph 4.1: The lecture opens by writing the second law as F_net = dp/dt, more general than ma. A is wrong: m v is momentum, not the second law. C is wrong: That is true only when the net external force on the system is zero, and even then it is a statement about total momentum, not about each force. D is wrong: That is not the second law.

questions.q: What is impulse, for a force acting over a time interval?
options: The force divided by the time
The change in kinetic energy only
The mass times the displacement
The accumulated effect of the force, equal to the integral of F dt, and equal to the change in momentum
questions.explain: Paragraph 4.2: The lecture defines impulse as that accumulated effect, J = Δp. A is wrong: Impulse is force accumulated over time, not divided by it. B is wrong: That is related to work, not to the definition of impulse. C is wrong: That is not impulse.

questions.q: When is the total momentum of a system conserved?
options: Only when the collision is elastic
Only when the bodies have equal mass
Whenever two bodies touch, even if a large external force acts on the system
When the net external force on the system as a whole is zero (or the external impulse is negligible)
questions.explain: Paragraph 4.3: The lecture states conservation of momentum under that condition. A is wrong: Conservation of momentum does not require elasticity; that is a condition on kinetic energy. B is wrong: Unequal masses can still conserve total momentum. C is wrong: A large external impulse changes the system's total momentum.

questions.q: How is the centre of mass of a system defined?
options: The position of the heaviest particle only
The geometric centre, even if the masses are unequal
The mass-weighted average of the positions of its parts
The point at which friction vanishes
questions.explain: Paragraph 4.4: The lecture defines the centre of mass that way, and later writes r_cm = Σ m_i r_i / Σ m_i. A is wrong: Every mass in the system is included, weighted by its mass. B is wrong: The average is mass-weighted, not purely geometric. D is wrong: The definition is about mass and position, not friction.

questions.q: A rocket, or a conveyor that drops sand, is a system whose mass is changing. How does the lecture treat the second law?
options: By setting F_net = ma with a fixed m, even as mass leaves the system
By ignoring momentum altogether
By writing a form such as m dv/dt = −v_ex dm/dt, with a relative exhaust (or dropped) speed
By assuming the exhaust speed is zero
questions.explain: Paragraph 4.6: The lecture gives that treatment of variable mass. A is wrong: The point is that mass is changing, so the more general form is needed. B is wrong: The second law is still a statement about momentum. D is wrong: A zero relative exhaust speed would give no thrust in that formula.

questions.q: How does the lecture classify collisions?
options: By what happens to the kinetic energy: elastic if K is conserved, inelastic if it is not, and perfectly inelastic if the bodies stick
By whether momentum is conserved
By whether the bodies have the same mass
By whether a force diagram can be drawn
questions.explain: Paragraph 4.7: The lecture says collisions are classified by kinetic energy, not by whether they 'look bouncey'. B is wrong: Momentum is conserved in all of these, when external impulse is negligible. C is wrong: Mass ratio is not the classification. D is wrong: A force diagram is always available; it is not the classification.

questions.q: A 1000 kg car moving at 20 m/s to the right collides and sticks with a car at rest. What principle gives the speed just after the collision?
options: Conservation of kinetic energy alone, which would leave the first car at 20 m/s
Conservation of momentum, with a common final speed v' = (m₁ v₁ + m₂ v₂) / (m₁ + m₂)
Setting both final velocities equal to zero
Newton's first law, applied to each car as if no force acted during the collision
questions.explain: Paragraph 4.9: The lecture works a perfectly inelastic example in that way. A is wrong: Kinetic energy is not conserved in a sticking collision. C is wrong: The combined wreck continues to the right. D is wrong: The cars exert large forces on each other during the collision; the first law does not apply to each separately in that interval.

questions.q: In the lecture's simplified ballistic pendulum, a projectile embeds in a hanging block. Which two conservation laws are used, and in which order?
options: Energy during the embedding, then momentum as the block rises
Only the first law, applied to the bullet alone
Momentum during the brief embedding (an inelastic collision), then mechanical energy as the combined mass rises
Only angular momentum about the Sun
questions.explain: Paragraph 4.13: The lecture treats that standard application in two stages, with those two laws. A is wrong: Those roles are reversed, and energy is not conserved in the embedding. B is wrong: The bullet and block interact strongly; the system must be chosen with care. D is wrong: The lecture's pendulum is a laboratory device, analysed with p and E.

questions.q: If a constant force F acts on a body that undergoes a displacement Δr, what is the work?
options: W = F / Δr
W = m v, in every case
W = F · Δr = F Δr cos θ, where θ is the angle between the force and the displacement
W = F t, even if the body does not move
questions.explain: Paragraph 5.2: The lecture defines work in that way, and warns that work is not a synonym for effort. A is wrong: Work is a product, not a quotient, of force and displacement. B is wrong: That is a confusion with momentum. D is wrong: If there is no displacement, this definition gives zero work.

questions.q: What does the work-energy theorem say?
options: The net work is always zero
The net work done on a body equals the change in its kinetic energy, ½ m v_f² − ½ m v_i²
Work equals the change in potential energy in every case, even for friction
Kinetic energy is conserved in every process
questions.explain: Paragraph 5.4: The lecture states the theorem in those terms. A is wrong: That is true only in special cases. C is wrong: That holds for conservative forces, treated later; the work-energy theorem is about kinetic energy. D is wrong: The theorem says kinetic energy changes by the net work.

questions.q: What is special about a conservative force, in this lecture?
options: It always does positive work
It depends on velocity, like drag
It cannot be included in a mechanical energy
The work it does between two points does not depend on the path, so a potential energy can be defined
questions.explain: Paragraph 5.6: The lecture introduces conservative forces by path-independence and the existence of a potential. A is wrong: Gravity can do negative work on a rising body. B is wrong: Drag is later named as non-conservative. C is wrong: The point of a conservative force is that it can.

questions.q: When is the mechanical energy of a system conserved?
options: Always, even when kinetic friction does work
Only when the body is at rest
When it is the sum of kinetic and potential energy, and the work of non-conservative forces is zero
Never, because energy cannot be defined in mechanics
questions.explain: Paragraph 5.8: The lecture defines mechanical energy as K + U and conserves it when W_nc = 0. A is wrong: Friction is non-conservative, and mechanical energy then changes. B is wrong: A moving pendulum can still conserve mechanical energy. D is wrong: The lecture is devoted to defining and using it.

questions.q: A roller-coaster car starts from rest at height h and rolls without friction. What is its speed at the bottom, if height is measured from there?
options: v = gh, with no square root
v = 0, because energy is conserved
v = sqrt(2gh), from mgh = ½ m v²
The speed depends on the car's mass in this frictionless case
questions.explain: Paragraph 5.9: The lecture gives that standard example and that conversion of potential energy into kinetic energy. A is wrong: The algebra of ½ m v² = mgh gives v = sqrt(2gh). B is wrong: Conservation moves the energy from U to K; it does not stop the car. D is wrong: Mass cancels; the lecture later asks why the speed is independent of mass and of path when W_nc = 0.

questions.q: A pendulum bob is pulled aside and released from rest. What is conserved, if the pivot is ideal and air resistance is neglected?
options: Mechanical energy: ½ m v² + m g y is constant
Horizontal momentum, because the string's tension is horizontal at every instant
The angle θ, because a pendulum never moves
Only kinetic energy, which is constant from the start
questions.explain: Paragraph 5.10: The lecture uses the pendulum as a clean energy example with that sum. B is wrong: The tension is along the string, not always horizontal, and there is an external force at the pivot. C is wrong: The bob moves; that is the point of the example. D is wrong: At release, K is zero and U is not; they exchange.

questions.q: What can you read from a potential-energy diagram, according to the lecture?
options: Only the mass of the particle
The same information as the energy equation: turning points where E = U, and where the motion is allowed because E ≥ U
The colour of the particle
The value of g at the Earth's centre
questions.explain: Paragraph 5.11: The lecture presents potential-energy diagrams as a third way to read that information. A is wrong: Mass is not what the diagram is for. C is wrong: That is not a mechanical quantity in the lecture. D is wrong: The diagram is a plot of U versus position for the system at hand.

questions.q: What is power, as the lecture defines it?
options: The rate at which work is done, or energy is transferred; for a force, P = F · v
The integral of force over distance, which is already work
The change in momentum
The moment of inertia of a rigid body
questions.explain: Paragraph 5.12: The lecture gives that definition and that instantaneous formula. B is wrong: Power is the rate of work, not work itself. C is wrong: That is impulse, or related to F Δt. D is wrong: That belongs to lecture six.

questions.q: What are the kinematic relations between linear and angular quantities, for a point at perpendicular distance r from a fixed axis?
options: s = rθ, v = rω, and a_t = rα, with θ in radians
s = θ/r, and v = ω/r
s = r + θ, as a sum of unlike quantities
Angular and linear quantities cannot be related
questions.explain: Paragraph 6.2: The lecture gives those analogues, with the radian as the natural unit. B is wrong: The radius multiplies the angular quantity, it does not divide it, in these relations. C is wrong: The relation is a product, and θ must be in radians. D is wrong: The lecture's point is that they can.

questions.q: What is the moment of inertia I of a rigid body about a given axis?
options: The sum (or integral) of m_i r_i², which depends on the axis as well as on the body
The body's mass alone, independent of how the mass is distributed
The angular velocity ω
The torque divided by the mass
questions.explain: Paragraph 6.4: The lecture defines I that way, and stresses the dependence on the axis. B is wrong: Two bodies of equal mass can have very different I. C is wrong: I is the inertial coefficient, not the motion. D is wrong: Torque equals Iα, so I is τ/α, not τ/m.

questions.q: What is Newton's second law for rotation about a fixed axis, or about the centre of mass?
options: The net torque equals I ω
The net torque equals I α
The net torque equals m v²/r
The net torque is always zero for a rolling body
questions.explain: Paragraph 6.6: The lecture states τ_net = Iα as the rotational analogue of F_net = ma. A is wrong: ω is angular velocity, not angular acceleration. C is wrong: That is a force or mass-times-acceleration relation for circular translation, not the rotation law itself. D is wrong: A body can roll with a nonzero α when a net torque acts.

questions.q: A skater with arms extended has I = 4 kg m² and a given angular speed, then pulls her arms in so that I falls to 2 kg m². If external torques are negligible, what happens?
options: Her angular speed is halved, to keep Iω² constant
Her angular speed is unchanged, because mass is unchanged
She stops spinning, because pulling the arms in is a dissipative process
Iω is conserved, so her angular speed doubles
questions.explain: Paragraph 6.8: The lecture works that conservation example in those numbers. A is wrong: The conserved quantity is Iω, not Iω². B is wrong: Mass is unchanged, but I is not, and ω changes. C is wrong: The lecture's point is that she spins faster.

questions.q: For a wheel of radius R that rolls without slipping, what relates v_cm and ω?
options: v_cm = ω / R
v_cm = ω R
v_cm = 0 whenever the wheel rotates
ω is always zero when the wheel translates
questions.explain: Paragraph 6.9: The lecture states rolling without slipping as the meeting of translation and rotation, with that constraint. A is wrong: The radius multiplies ω, it does not divide it. C is wrong: The centre of mass moves; it is the contact point that is instantaneously at rest. D is wrong: That would be sliding without rotation, not rolling without slipping.

questions.q: What is the kinetic energy of a rigid body, in the lecture's decomposition?
options: ½ M v_cm² only, even if the body is spinning
½ I ω² only, even if the centre of mass is moving
The kinetic energy of the centre of mass, ½ M v_cm², plus the rotational kinetic energy about the centre of mass, ½ I_cm ω²
M g h only
questions.explain: Paragraph 6.10: The lecture states that sum, and applies it to a rolling disk. A is wrong: The rotational term is required when the body rotates. B is wrong: The translational term is required when the centre of mass moves. D is wrong: That is a potential energy, not the kinetic energy of a rigid body.

questions.q: A body rolls without slipping down a slope. Why do a disk and a hoop, released together, not reach the bottom together?
options: A larger I, such as the hoop's I = M R² compared with the disk's ½ M R², stores more energy in rotation, so the centre of mass is slower at a given height; equivalently a = g sinθ / (1 + I/(M R²))
Gravity is stronger on the hoop
The hoop has no moment of inertia
Rolling without slipping is impossible on a slope
questions.explain: Paragraph 6.11: The lecture gives both the energy comparison and that acceleration formula. B is wrong: Gravity is mg on both. C is wrong: The hoop's I is M R², larger than the disk's. D is wrong: The lecture analyses exactly that motion.
